title: Recover a Tree From Preorder Traversal Problem

notes: The returned tree is serialized in level-order, omitting trailing null values.
The traversal contains only non-negative decimal node values separated from depth information by dashes; the root has depth 0.
constraints: The number of nodes in the original tree is in the range [1, 1000].
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: Read each node's depth from its leading dashes. The stack stores the current root-to-node path, so nodes at depth 2 become children of the node at depth 1, and the later depth-1 node becomes the root's right child.
After reading node 4 at depth 3, the next depth-1 node causes the stack to pop back to the root. The depth-2 node 6 then becomes the right child of 5, with 7 nested under 6.
The depth sequence 0,1,2,3,2 determines the parent changes. Node 90 is the left child of 349, and node 88 is the right child of 349.

content.problemStatement:
We run a preorder depth-first search (DFS) on the `root` of a binary tree.

At each node in this traversal, we output `D` dashes (where `D` is the depth of this node), then we output the value of this node.  If the depth of a node is `D`, the depth of its immediate child is `D + 1`.  The depth of the `root` node is `0`.

If a node has only one child, that child is guaranteed to be **the left child**.

With the output `traversal` of this traversal, recover the tree and output *its* `root`.

**Example 1:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2024/09/10/recover_tree_ex1.png)

```
Input: traversal = "1-2--3--4-5--6--7"
Output: [1,2,5,3,4,6,7]
```

**Example 2:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2024/09/10/recover_tree_ex2.png)

```
Input: traversal = "1-2--3---4-5--6---7"
Output: [1,2,5,3,null,6,null,4,null,7]
```

**Example 3:**

![](https://assets.leetcode.com/uploads/2024/09/10/recover_tree_ex3.png)

```
Input: traversal = "1-401--349---90--88"
Output: [1,401,null,349,88,90]
```

**Constraints:**

* The number of nodes in the original tree is in the range `[1, 1000]`.
* `1 <= Node.val <= 10^9`

notes: The intended solution is linear in the traversal length. The auxiliary stack is O(h), where h is the tree height.
The depth uniquely determines when ancestors must be removed from the current path.
The guarantee that a single child is always the left child makes the left-then-right attachment rule sufficient.
solution.approach: Parse the traversal from left to right while maintaining a stack containing the current root-to-node path. For each node, count its leading dashes to get its depth, parse its value, pop the stack until its size equals that depth, and attach the new node to the remaining top node. If the parent's left child is empty, attach there; otherwise attach to the right. The first node is the root.

better.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) recursion stack, plus the constructed tree.
better.description: Use one shared parsing index with recursive descent. The recursive function expects a specific depth, consumes the next node only when its dash count matches that depth, and recursively attempts the left and right children at depth + 1. Each traversal character is consumed once.

optimal.complexity: O(n) time and O(h) auxiliary stack space, plus O(n) space for the constructed tree.
optimal.description: Use an iterative stack representing the current root-to-node path. Count dashes to obtain the node depth, pop until the stack size equals that depth, attach the new node to the stack top, then push it. The left-child guarantee means the first child occupies left and the second occupies right.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n^2) worst-case time and O(h) recursion stack, plus the constructed tree.
bruteForce.description: A straightforward recursive approach can scan forward to identify the range belonging to each subtree and recursively recover its children. If subtree boundaries are repeatedly searched by scanning the remaining traversal, the same characters may be examined many times.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n), where n is the length of the traversal string.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) including the constructed tree; O(h) auxiliary stack space, where h is the tree height.

followUps: Can you implement the recovery recursively using a shared parsing index?
How does the auxiliary space change for a highly skewed tree?
Can the parser be adapted to handle a larger number of nodes without recursive call-stack growth?
What changes would be needed if a node with one child were allowed to have that child on either side?
